lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Hook, Line and Sinker
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 3, Session 1
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 3 Session 1

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA03 how persuasive texts are organised into stages (the opening); VC2E5LY10 creating texts for purpose and audience; VC2E5LE04 experimenting with imagery
plan.shape: model five, battle, write five: students see one issue opened five ways, battle hooks in pairs, then write five of their own and choose, because choice and competition lift effort late in the year
plan.criticalFeature: a hook makes the reader need the next sentence, and the best hook fits the audience
decisionPoints: the choice check: the best hook for the principal
the exit board: a new hook, named
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today: sell it from the very first line.
plan.catchUp: Missed earlier weeks? Give the Hook Starters page and the issue Should zoos keep polar bears? They write five hooks for that.

studentTools: Writing books with the Week 1 Issue Card
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Five hook names down the side of the board: question, shocking fact, imagine, mini-story, bold statement
A Hook Battle bracket for the class vote

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: name hooks, match a hook to a reader, write hooks for new issues, then five for your own.
resources.title: Hook, Line and Sinker
resources.subtitle: A hook makes your reader need the next sentence.

example.prompt: 'Picture a playground with no shade at all.'
steps: Match: question, fact, imagine, story or bold

items.prompt: Write the type of each hook: question, shocking fact, imagine, mini-story or bold statement.
rows: What if your lunchbox could save a turtle?
Yesterday, a koala crossed our school oval.
Australians use billions of plastic bags each year.
Imagine a summer with no beach days.
answers: What if your lunchbox could save a turtle?
Yesterday, a koala crossed our school oval.
Australians use billions of plastic bags each year.
Imagine a summer with no beach days.

example.prompt: Reader: a Prep class. Issue: litter.
example.answer: 'Can you help a hungry magpie?' Simple and about animals.

items.prompt: Reader: Year 3. Issue: litter. Best hook?
options: Can a lolly wrapper trap a lizard?
items.explain: A question about an animal, in simple words, pulls young readers in.

items.prompt: Noah wrote this hook. Find the problem and fix it.
work: This is about litter. I will tell you why litter is bad.
items.answer: It announces the topic but doesn't pull. Fix: Every lunchtime, our oval swallows another fifty wrappers.

example.prompt: Issue: should we ban single-use cups? Type: imagine.
steps: Make them need the next line
example.answer: Imagine a mountain of cups taller than our school.

items.prompt: Write the hook for each issue, using the type given.
rows: Should every school have solar panels?
answers: What if one extra hour of sleep made every lesson easier?
The bear paced to the fence, turned, and paced back.
Should every school have solar panels?
The sun hits our school roof with free energy every single day.

steps: Star the best for your reader
example.answer: Five hooks, one starred: 'It works because my reader...'

items.prompt: Write five hooks for your own issue, one of each type. Star the best one for your reader and write why.
items.answer: Five labelled hooks, one starred, with a reason that names the reader.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: combine hooks, then make the ending echo the opening.
resources.title: Hook Master
resources.subtitle: The best openings use two hooks at once.

example.prompt: Story + question: The bear paced back and forth. Would you call that living?
steps: Check it pulls harder than either alone
example.answer: A mini-story that ends in a question.

items.prompt: Combine the two hook types for each issue.
rows: Should kids have a later bedtime?
Should our town have a dog park?
answers: Straws can last hundreds of years. Is one drink worth that?
Should kids have a later bedtime?
Imagine waking up rested. Kids need an extra hour.
Should our town have a dog park?
Max pulled at his lead all the way home. Where can he run?

example.prompt: Hook: Imagine a beach you can't see for plastic. Echo: Let's keep our beaches golden.
steps: Bring it back at the end
example.answer: The last line returns to the beach.

items.prompt: Write your best opening (two hooks combined), then the last line of your conclusion that echoes it.
items.answer: A combined opening and an ending that brings back its picture or words.

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we learn to hook a reader so hard they can't stop reading.

slides.title: For the teacher: Week 3 at a glance
lines: This week: play with persuasion. Hooks, devices, a letter in role, a campaign poster.
Today: five kinds of hook, a hook battle, five hooks for their own issue.
Session 4 is the draw and create fun activity: a campaign poster (print one A3 sheet each if you can).
Unit anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it.
slides.notes: Teacher-facing only. Skip it in front of the class.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Draw the five hook names and a battle bracket on the board.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write an opening hook that makes the reader need to keep reading.
successCriteria: I can name five kinds of hook.
I can write a hook that fits my issue and my reader.
I can choose my best hook and explain why it works.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Readers decide in one sentence whether to keep going.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Naming the hooks is where we start.
Writing a hook that fits your reader is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 naming hooks is reachable for all; SC2 writing a fitting hook is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 choosing and justifying is the stretch.

slides.title: Which video would you watch?
lines: Hello. Today I will talk about bins.
There's a monster under our school, and it eats 40 kilograms of lunch every week.

notes.answer: the second - you need to know what the monster is
beats: SAY: Two videos about the same thing.
You only have time to watch one.
ASK: Which would you watch, first or second?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1 or 2... show me.
EXPECT: 2
ASK: Why can't you stop at the first sentence of video two?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: you want to know what the monster is
SAY: The monster is our rubbish bin. Week 1 you wrote openings.
Today we make the first line impossible to ignore.
trap: choosing the first because it is clear.
Fix: ask would you keep reading? Student re-votes honestly.
notes.prep: Launch reconnects to the Week 1 opening paragraph. The bin figure is invented for the hook; say so if asked. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: An opening line that grabs the reader and won't let go.
slides.example: Imagine walking the same twenty steps, every day, for thirty years.

notes.answer: an opening line that grabs the reader and won't let go
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Hook. Say it with me. Hook.
SAY: A hook is your first line. It pulls the reader in like a magnet.
Hook, line and sinker: they swallow the whole thing.
ASK: Does the example make you want the next sentence? Why?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: yes, who walks twenty steps? why?
trap: thinking a hook means a joke.
Fix: say a hook can be serious, shocking or sad. It just has to pull.
notes.prep: The word the session runs on. The example previews the zoo model.

rows: Would you want to spend your whole life in a backyard?
Some wild polar bears roam areas bigger than Tasmania.
Imagine walking the same twenty steps, every day, for thirty years.
The bear paced to the wall, turned, and paced back. Again.
A zoo is no place for a polar bear.

notes.answer: five hooks for one issue; pick the one that fits the reader
beats: SAY: My issue: should zoos keep polar bears? I'll open it five ways.
READ each hook aloud, slowly.
POINT to Shocking fact.
SAY: This one's true and surprising. Bigger than Tasmania. I'd use it for adults.
POINT to Mini-story.
SAY: This one makes you feel it. I'd use it for kids my age.
ASK: Which hook would you choose for our principal?
10 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1 to 5... show me.
EXPECT: 2 or 5. ACCEPT: any with a reason
trap: choosing the hook they like, not the one the reader would like.
Fix: ask who's reading? Student re-chooses for that reader.
notes.stretch: Combine two hooks into one opening.
notes.help: Start with the bold statement: it's the easiest to write.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: a hook makes the reader need the next sentence, and fits the audience.
notes.sources: SOURCES: polar bear home ranges vary widely; some exceed Tasmania's area (Polar Bears International).

slides.title: Name that hook
slides.pivot: read the first two words; they usually give it away
slides.followUp: cold call one student: what gave it away?

items.text: Have you ever wondered where your chip packet goes after the bin?
Every minute, about a garbage truck of plastic enters the ocean.
Imagine a beach where you can't see the sand for plastic.
Last week, a girl at the beach untangled a plastic bag from a seagull's leg.

say: 1 question, 2 shocking fact, 3 imagine, 4 mini-story, 5 bold.
trap: calling the mini-story a fact because it could be true.
Fix: ask is it telling what happened to someone? Then it's a story.
notes.stretch: Say which hook fits a Prep audience best.
notes.help: Check the first two words against the board.
notes.prep: Guided naming on a new topic. SC1. Garbage truck a minute: Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 2016.

slides.title: Which hook would grab the principal?
slides.prompt: Issue: we need a longer lunch break.

options.text: Hi, my name is Sam and this is about lunch.
options.misconception: introduces the writer, not the issue; nothing pulls

options.text: What if ten extra minutes made every afternoon calmer?
LUNCH IS WAY TOO SHORT AND IT IS NOT FAIR!!!
options.misconception: shouting, not hooking; doesn't fit a principal

notes.answer: B - a question about what the principal cares about
beats: SAY: Think about who's reading: the principal.
ASK: Which hook would grab the principal?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: why calmer afternoons?
Less -> ask what does a principal want? re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. It's a question about calmer afternoons, which principals care about.
trap: pointing to C because it shows strong feeling.
Fix: ask would the principal keep reading? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Decision point: audience fit. Under 80% means the battle uses the principal as the judge.

slides.title: Hook battle!
lines: Issue: should our school ban junk food at the canteen?
Write your best hook in 60 seconds.
Battle your partner. The winners go head to head.

notes.answer: open - any hook type that fits the reader
beats: SAY: One issue. Sixty seconds. Your best hook.
ASK: Write your best hook on your board.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: questions, facts, imagine lines
ASK: Read hooks to your partner. Point to the one that pulls harder.
20 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to the winning board.
EXPECT: one winner per pair
ASK: Four winners read aloud. Which would you keep reading?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Thumbs up on your pick... now.
EXPECT: one clear class winner
trap: Fix: read the four hooks anonymously, teacher reads aloud.
notes.stretch: Write a second hook of a different type for the same issue.
notes.help: Use a Hook Starter: Have you ever wondered...?
notes.prep: Oral and written rehearsal with a competitive edge, 8 minutes. SC2.

slides.title: Five hooks for your issue
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish with five hooks for your own issue, the best one starred.
slides.frame: My best hook works because my reader ___.

notes.answer: five labelled hooks, one starred with a reason that names the reader
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Your issue from Week 1. Five ways in. Then you choose.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: who's your reader? Does your star fit them?
ASK: How many of your five hooks are done?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: 3 or more at the halfway mark
TIME 15 minutes. At 12, two students read their starred hook.
trap: five hooks of the same kind.
Fix: student labels each hook with its type, rewrites any doubles.
notes.stretch: Extension: combine two hooks, then echo the opening at the end.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, starters to finish, a frame.
notes.prep: Independent application. The starred hook opens their big piece in Week 4. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in five hooks for the student's issue, the best starred and justified

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: New issue: should every school have a vegetable garden?
Write one hook. Then write which kind it is.

notes.answer: any hook that pulls, labelled correctly, e.g. Imagine eating a tomato you grew yourself
beats: SAY: A brand new issue. Hook me.
ASK: Write a hook and name its kind.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: e.g. What if lunch grew outside our classroom? Question.
RECORD who writes a statement that doesn't pull. Tomorrow's warm-up.
trap: Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new issue. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read your starred hook to your partner. Did they want the next sentence?

notes.answer: open - listen for a hook that fits its reader
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can write a hook that fits your reader?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Read your starred hook. Did your partner want more?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: yes, they asked what happened next
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. SC2.
